subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: If the normal at one end of a latus rectum of the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with eccentricity e, passes through one end of the minor axis, then show that e⁴ + e² = 1.

mark_split.label: Equation of the normal at the end of the latus rectum
Substitute the end of the minor axis

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.65 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 76. NOT on an SSP page. Printed appearance: TS 17 only — no AP tag. Book p.65 prints tick boxes with no numeric mark tags, so the 1+1+1+1 split here is OURS, following the four natural stages of the proof. Ellipse is an SAQ-ONLY unit on the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.5). No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE BLM on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 are the orchestrator's back-test stand-in).

insider_note: The identity b² = a²(1 − e²) is what turns ab = a² − b² into ab = a²e² — writing that substitution as its own line, rather than doing it mentally, is where most students lose a mark in a rushed answer.

steps.label: Equation of the normal at the end of the latus rectum
steps.margin_note: First mark. L = (ae, b²/a) is the end of the latus rectum used here.
steps.memory_tip: The general normal formula a²x/x₁ − b²y/y₁ = a² − b² works at any point (x₁, y₁) on the ellipse — substitute L into it.
lines: Equation of the normal at (x₁, y₁): a²x/x₁ − b²y/y₁ = a² − b²
Let L = (ae, b²/a) be the end of the latus rectum
Normal at L: a²x/(ae) − b²y/(b²/a) = a² − b² ⇒ ax/e − ay = a² − b² …(1)
steps.why: The general normal formula applies at any point on the ellipse, so substituting the specific point L directly gives the normal at the end of the latus rectum.
common_mistakes: Using the OTHER end of the latus rectum, (ae, −b²/a), instead of the positive one.
Simplifying b²y/(b²/a) incorrectly — it should become ay, not by.

steps.label: Substitute the end of the minor axis
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The end of the minor axis meant here is B′(0, −b), the lower end.
steps.memory_tip: There are two ends of the minor axis — the book uses the one that makes the algebra work out to a positive equation.
lines: This normal passes through B′(0, −b), one end of the minor axis:
a(0)/e − a(−b) = a² − b² ⇒ ab = a² − b²
steps.why: The condition 'the normal passes through one end of the minor axis' becomes an algebraic equation once the coordinates of that end are substituted into the normal's equation (1).
common_mistakes: Using B(0, b) instead of B′(0, −b), which changes the sign of the resulting equation.
Losing the negative sign when substituting y = −b into −ay.

steps.label: Simplify to ab = a²e²
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Replace b² using b² = a²(1 − e²).
steps.memory_tip: b² = a²(1 − e²) is the single most useful substitution in this whole chapter — it connects a, b and e.
lines: ab = a² − b² = a² − a²(1 − e²) [since b² = a²(1 − e²)]
steps.why: Replacing b² with a²(1 − e²) turns the equation ab = a² − b² into one written purely in terms of a and e, ready for the final step.
common_mistakes: Expanding a² − a²(1 − e²) incorrectly and losing the a²e² term.
Forgetting to divide both sides by a at all — the a on the left must stay to match a²e² on the right.

steps.label: Conclude e⁴ + e² = 1
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Divide by a, square, and use b² = a²(1 − e²) once more.
steps.memory_tip: Once e² = b/a is known, squaring gives e⁴ = b²/a² — substitute b² = a²(1 − e²) one more time to finish.
steps.why: Squaring e² = b/a gives e⁴ = b²/a², and substituting b² = a²(1 − e²) once more shows this equals 1 − e², which rearranges directly to the required identity.
common_mistakes: Dividing ab = a²e² by a² instead of by a, which gives b/a = ae² instead of e² = b/a.
Stopping at e⁴ = 1 − e² without writing the final rearranged form e⁴ + e² = 1.
